title: The better land promised to the righteous
source_text: Μετὰ (δὲ) τὰ περὶ θεοῦ, ἐν οἷς ἡμᾶς συκοφαντεῖ, πυνθάνεται ἡμῶν· ποῖ ἀπεῖναι μέλλομεν; καὶ τίνα ἐλπίδα ἔχομεν; καὶ ὡς ἀποκριναμένων, τίθησι δῆθεν ἡμετέρας φωνὰς οὕτως ἐχούσας· εἰς ἄλλην γῆν, ταύτης κρείττονα. καὶ πρὸς τοῦτό φησιν· ἱστόρηται θείοις ἀνδράσι παλαιοῖς εὐδαίμων βίος ψυχαῖς εὐδαίμοσιν· ὠνόμασαν δὲ [οἱ δὲ] οἱ μὲν μακάρων νήσους. οἱ δὲ „Ἠλύσιον πεδίον“ ἀπὸ τῆς λύσεως τῶν ἔνθεν κακῶν, ὥσπερ καὶ Ὅμηρος· ἀλλά σ᾿ ἐς Ἠλύσιον πεδίον καὶ πείρατα γαίης ἀθάνατοι πέμψουσι, τῇ περ ῥηίστη βιοτή. Πλάτων δὲ ἀθάνατον τὴν ψυχὴν ἡγούμενος ἐκείνην τὴν χώραν, ἔνθα στέλλεται, ἄντικρυς „γῆν“ ὠνόμασεν οὕτως· „πάμμεγά τι εἶναι“ φήσας „αὐτὸ, καὶ ἡμᾶς οἰκεῖν τοὺς μέχρι Ἡρακλείων στηλῶν ἀπὸ Φάσιδος ἐν σμικρῷ τινι μορίῳ. ὥσπερ περὶ τέλμα μύρμηκας ἢ βατράχους περὶ τὴν θάλασσαν οἰκοῦντας, καὶ ἄλλους ἄλλοθι πολλοὺς ἐν (πολλοῖς) τοιούτοις τόποις οἰκεῖν. εἶναι γὰρ πανταχῇ περὶ τὴν γῆν πολλὰ κοῖλα καὶ παντοδαπὰ καὶ τὰς ἰδέας καὶ τὰ μεγέθη, εἰς ἃ συνεῤῥυηκέναι τό τε ὕδωρ καὶ τὴν ὁμίχλην καὶ τὸν ἀέρα· αὐτὴν δὲ τὴν γῆν καθαρὰν ἐν καθαρῷ κεῖσθαι τῷ οὐρανῷ.“ ὑπολαμβάνει τοίνυν ὁ Κέλσος τὰ περὶ τῆς ἄλλης γῆς κρείττονος καὶ πολλῷ ταύτης διαφερούσης εἰληφέναι ἡμᾶς ἀπό τινων νομιζομένων αὐτῷ θείων παλαιῶν ἀνδρῶν καὶ μάλιστα Πλάτωνος, τοῦ ἐν τῷ Φαίδωνι περὶ γῆς καθαρᾶς ἐν καθαρῷ κειμένης οὐρανῷ φιλοσοφήσαντος· οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι Μωϋσῆς, ὁ πολλῷ καὶ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν γραμμάτων ἀρχαιότερος, εἰσήγαγε τὸν θεὸν ἐπαγγελλόμενον τὴν ἁγίαν γῆν καὶ „ἀγαθὴν καὶ πολλὴν, ῥέουσαν γάλα καὶ μέλι“ τοῖς κατὰ τὸν νόμον ἑαυτοῦ βιώσασιν, οὐδ᾿ ὡς οἴονταί τινες τὴν „ἀγαθὴν,“ τὴν κάτω νομιζομένην Ἰουδαίαν, κειμένην καὶ αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ ἀρχῆθεν κατηραμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις τῆς παραβάσεως τοῦ Ἀδὰμ γῇ. τὸ γὰρ „ἐπικατάρατος ἡ γῆ ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις σου· ἐν λύπαις φαγῇ αὐτὴν πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς σου“ περὶ ὅλης εἴρηται τῆς γῆς, ἣν „ἐν λύπαις,“ τουτέστι πόνοις, ἐσθίει πᾶς ἄνθρωπος „ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ“ ἀποθανὼν, καὶ ἐσθίει „πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς“ ἑαυτοῦ „ζωῆς.“ καὶ ὡς „ἐπικατάρατος“ πᾶσα ἡ γῆ „ἀκάνθας καὶ τριβόλους ἀνατελεῖ“ „πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς“ τοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ ἐκβληθέντος ἀπὸ τοῦ παραδείσου, καὶ „ἐν ἱδρῶτι τοῦ προσώπου“ ἑαυτοῦ ἐσθίει πᾶς ἄνθρωπος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἄρτον. „ἕως ἐπιστρέψει εἰς τὴν γῆν, ἐξ ἧς ἐλήφθη.“ πολὺν μὲν οὖν ἔχει λόγον ὅλα τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον τοῦτον, δυνάμενον εἰς τὴν σαφήνειαν τῶν λέξεων κατασκευασθῆναι· ὀλίγοις δ᾿ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ἠρκέσθημεν, βουλόμενοι ἀπολῦσαι περισπασμοῦ, τοῦ ὡς περὶ τῆς Ἰουδαίας γῆς ὑπολαμβάνοντος εἰρῆσθαι τὰ περὶ ἀγαθῆς γῆς. ἣν ὁ θεὸς ὑπισχνεῖται τοῖς δικαίοις.
pass_a_gloss: After the things about God, in which he slanders (συκοφαντέω) us, he inquires (πυνθάνομαι) of us: where are we going to depart (ἄπειμι)? and what hope (ἐλπίς) do we have? And as if we had answered, he sets down supposedly (δῆθεν) our words (φωναί) running thus: to another land (γῆ), better (κρείττων) than this. And to this he says: a happy (εὐδαίμων) life (βίος) for happy souls has been recounted (ἱστορέω) by divine (θεῖοι) men of old; some named it Isles (νῆσοι) of the Blessed (μάκαρες), others 'Elysian Plain (Ἠλύσιον πεδίον)' from the release (λύσις) from the evils here (ἔνθεν), as also Homer: 'but you to the Elysian plain and the limits (πείρατα) of earth the immortals (ἀθάνατοι) will send, where (τῇ περ) life (βιοτή) is easiest (ῥηίστη).' And Plato, holding the soul immortal (ἀθάνατος), named (ὀνομάζω) outright (ἄντικρυς) that region (χώρα) whither it is sent (στέλλω) 'earth' thus: saying 'it is something very great (πάμμεγας), and we who dwell from Phasis up to the Pillars (στῆλαι) of Heracles dwell in some small part (μόριον), like ants (μύρμηκες) or frogs (βάτραχοι) around a marsh (τέλμα) dwelling around the sea, and many others elsewhere dwell in many such places. For there are everywhere around the earth many hollows (κοῖλα) of all kinds both in forms (ἰδέαι) and sizes (μεγέθη), into which water and mist (ὁμίχλη) and air (ἀήρ) have flowed together (συρρέω); but the earth itself lies (κεῖμαι) pure (καθαρός) in pure heaven (οὐρανός).' Celsus then supposes (ὑπολαμβάνω) that we have taken the things about the other land, better and far differing from this, from some men thought by him divine and old, and most of all Plato, who in the Phaedo philosophized (φιλοσοφέω) about a pure earth lying in pure heaven; not seeing that Moses, much older (ἀρχαιότερος) even than Greek letters/writings (γράμματα), introduced (εἰσάγω) God promising (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) the holy (ἅγιος) land and 'good (ἀγαθή) and large (πολλή), flowing (ῥέω) milk and honey' to those who lived according to his law; not, as some think, the 'good' [land] as the Judaea reckoned (νομίζω) below (κάτω), lying itself also in the earth cursed (καταράομαι) from the beginning (ἀρχῆθεν) in the works (ἔργα) of the transgression (παράβασις) of Adam. For 'cursed (ἐπικατάρατος) is the earth in your works; in sorrows (λῦπαι) you shall eat it all the days of your life' was said about the whole earth, which 'in sorrows,' that is, toils (πόνοι), every man having died 'in Adam' eats, and eats 'all the days of' his own 'life.' And as 'cursed,' the whole earth 'will raise up (ἀνατέλλω) thorns (ἄκανθαι) and thistles (τρίβολοι)' 'all the days of the life' of the one cast out (ἐκβάλλω) in Adam from the paradise (παράδεισος), and 'in the sweat (ἱδρώς) of the face (πρόσωπον)' of himself every man eats his own bread (ἄρτος) 'until he returns (ἐπιστρέφω) to the earth from which he was taken (λαμβάνω).' Much reasoning (λόγος) all the things in this passage (τόπος) have, able to be worked out (κατασκευάζω) for the clarity (σαφήνεια) of the words; but for the present we were content (ἀρκέομαι) with few, wishing to release (ἀπολύω) from distraction (περισπασμός) the one supposing that the things about a good land, which God promises (ὑπισχνέομαι) to the righteous, were said about the land of Judaea.
pass_b_english: After what he says about God, in which he slanders us, he asks us where we expect to go, and what hope we have. And as though we had answered, he sets down supposed words of ours, which run: “To another land, better than this one.” To this he says: “Divine men of old have told of a happy life for happy souls. Some named it the Islands of the Blessed, others the Elysian Plain, from the release from the evils of this world, as Homer too says: ‘But the immortals will send you to the Elysian Plain and the ends of the earth, where life is easiest’ (Homer, Odyssey 4.563–565). And Plato, who holds the soul to be immortal, openly calls that region to which it is sent a ‘land,’ in these words: ‘that it is something very great, and that we who dwell from the Phasis to the Pillars of Heracles inhabit a small part of it, living around the sea like ants or frogs around a marsh, and that many others dwell elsewhere in many such places. For everywhere around the earth there are many hollows of every kind, in shape and in size, into which water, mist and air have flowed together; but the earth itself lies pure in the pure heaven’ (Plato, Phaedo 109a–c).”

Celsus supposes, then, that we have taken what we say about the other land, better than this one and far superior to it, from certain men whom he regards as divine men of old, and above all from Plato, who in the Phaedo discoursed as a philosopher about a pure earth lying in the pure heaven. He does not see that Moses, who is far older even than the writings of the Greeks, brought in God promising the holy land, “good and broad, flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8), to those who had lived according to his law; and not, as some think, promising as the “good” land the Judaea that is reckoned to be here below, which itself also lies within the earth that was cursed from the beginning in the works of Adam’s transgression.

For the words “Cursed is the earth in your works; in sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:17) were spoken about the whole earth. Every man who has died “in Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:22) eats of it “in sorrows,” that is, in toils, and he eats of it “all the days of” his “life.” And because the whole earth is “cursed,” it “will bring forth thorns and thistles” (Genesis 3:18) “all the days of the life” of him who was cast out of paradise in Adam (Genesis 3:23–24); and every man eats his bread “in the sweat of” his “face, until he returns to the earth from which he was taken” (Genesis 3:19).

Everything in this passage calls for long discussion, which could be worked out to make its words clear. For the present we have been content with a few remarks, wishing to free from distraction anyone who supposes that what is said about the good land which God promises to the righteous was said about the land of Judaea.

choices.choice: Celsus’s question (‘where are we to go, what hope do we have’) is reported by Origen in the first person plural and is rendered as indirect speech; the answer Celsus puts in Christian mouths (‘To another land, better than this one’) is in double quotation marks as Celsus’s framing. Celsus’s own reply runs from ἱστόρηται to the end of the Plato quotation and is in double quotation marks, with Homer and Plato in single quotation marks inside it. The copy-text’s bracketed [οἱ δὲ] before οἱ μὲν is deleted by the editor and is not translated. Ἠλύσιον is etymologised from λύσις (‘release’); the play cannot be kept in English and is rendered ‘from the release from the evils of this world’ (τῶν ἔνθεν κακῶν, ‘the evils of here’). The Isles of the Blessed are not quoted from a named author (compare Hesiod, Works and Days 171), so no source is given. Homer, Odyssey 4.563–565 is quoted with line 564 (ὅθι ξανθὸς Ῥαδάμανθυς) left out and πέλει ἀνθρώποισιν dropped from 565; translated as Celsus gives it. Plato, Phaedo 109a–c: the copy-text has θάλασσαν for Plato’s θάλατταν; (πολλοῖς) is an editorial supplement agreeing with the Plato manuscripts and is translated. The copy-text’s full stops before ὥσπερ and before ἣν ὁ θεός are read as commas. Exodus 3:8 Septuagint: εἰς γῆν ἀγαθὴν καὶ πολλήν, εἰς γῆν ῥέουσαν γάλα καὶ μέλι (also Exodus 3:17); πολλήν is rendered ‘broad’. Genesis 3:17 Septuagint ἐπικατάρατος ἡ γῆ ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις σου (‘in your works’), where the Hebrew has ‘because of you’; ἐν λύπαις (‘in sorrows’). ‘In Adam’ is from 1 Corinthians 15:22. Genesis 3:19: Origen adapts the second person to the third (‘his face’, ‘until he returns ... from which he was taken’); the Septuagint has ἕως τοῦ ἀποστρέψαι σε. ‘Cast out of paradise’ alludes to Genesis 3:23–24. τοῦ ... ὑπολαμβάνοντος after περισπασμοῦ is read as ‘anyone who supposes’ (the person freed from distraction); the genitive is awkward and may stand for an accusative. Ἑλληνικῶν γραμμάτων may mean Greek writings or the Greek alphabet; rendered ‘the writings of the Greeks’.
